suggestions.quote: The cousin's wedding, the flat's loan, a startup: tap, tap, tap.
suggestions.fix: This is three new sets in one beat and the likeliest long pole. Stage it as one phone-in-hand insert with the hourglass, with a backdrop layer swapped per tap (a string of wedding lights, a loan stamp, a laptop sticker). Show each tap as one clear aging stage on the rig: grey hair, then glasses, then stoop.

The outline never names the rule device. Make the hourglass the device. Each tap drains a measure of sand and greys the world a step, while you and your father keep colour. That shows the rule whenever it applies, and it gives the sound seat a sound to key on.

suggestions.quote: a nurse asks which of you is the patient
suggestions.fix: Stage side-on on the bench with two grey-haired figures. Put the nurse's question in a bubble of four words: BUBBLE nurse: "Which is the patient?". Add a worried-then-shocked face on you within 2 s. Plan the father's teasing bus-pass beat (line 36) as a bubble too: "Still using that pass?"

suggestions.quote: your father won't let you pay for his medicine any more
suggestions.fix: This is a two-figure scene with the father speaking only in a bubble. Use "No. Keep your years." (four words). Stage it as a hand pushing the phone away. That gives one clear gesture and keeps the trigger gesture (finger over the button) consistent with line 34.

suggestions.quote: Your hours as a pile of years
suggestions.fix: A pile of years is the hardest picture to stage in this outline. Draw it as stacked paper calendar sheets or a split-flap counter of years, not a new set. Keep one thing moving every 2 to 4 s (the counter ticks, the stack grows).

suggestions.quote: Last line inside the image: the next time you price something, price it in hours
suggestions.fix: Keep this line spoken. If it is also on screen, use a stamped tag at the left, not the right third, because the last 15 s keep the right third quiet for end screens.
